canonical_topic: Fair value leveling example: Henry Hub vs. Texas gas basis
definition: A worked example showing how the level 1/2/3 fair-value hierarchy applies to natural gas prices and derivatives, using Henry Hub as the level 1 benchmark and Texas basis-priced gas as level 2.
core_idea: Henry Hub is the primary U.S. natural gas price benchmark and futures delivery point, so its prices and futures are level 1. Texas gas is priced as a basis spread to Henry Hub (broker-quoted, typically a couple of cents), making that spread a level 2 input and any swap settling in Texas a level 2 security because it blends a level 1 input with a level 2 input.
key_points: Henry Hub is the delivery point for U.S. natural gas futures and the national benchmark price.
Prices observed directly at Henry Hub are level 1 inputs; futures settling there are level 1 securities.
Texas natural gas is priced as a spread (basis) to Henry Hub, typically within a couple of cents.
That basis spread is quoted primarily by brokers, which makes it a level 2 input.
A swap settling in Texas is a level 2 security because it combines a level 1 input (Henry Hub price) with a level 2 input (the basis spread).
relationships: Depends on the level 1/2/3 fair-value input hierarchy defined elsewhere in this section.
trading_implications: Valuing Texas-delivered gas positions requires both a Henry Hub reference price and a broker-quoted basis, so the valuation is only as reliable as the basis quote source.
caveats: A security is not automatically level 1 just because it references a level 1 price if any part of its valuation also relies on a level 2 (or lower) input.
